bib.title: Chapter 1: Analyzing Text Data with Deep Learning (Building AI Agents with LLMs, RAG, and Knowledge Graphs)

question: How is text turned into numerical representations and analysed with RNN, LSTM, GRU and CNN models, ending in a sentiment classifier?
contributions: Walks from one-hot, BoW and TF-IDF to word2vec embeddings, then RNN/LSTM/GRU/1D-CNN, then a GRU sentiment classifier.

Chapter says its tutorial leads into the next chapter's limits of these models; transformers not covered here.
practices: Lowercase and normalise text before tokenizing; consider lemmatization or stemming (Representing text for AI).
Prefer TF-IDF over raw counts: log-scale term frequency and weight by inverse document frequency (TF-IDF).
Use dense embeddings (word2vec, ~300 dims) instead of sparse count vectors; mix Wikipedia and news data (Embedding section).
Use cosine similarity rather than raw dot product to compare vectors (A notion of similarity for text).
Visualise embeddings with UMAP, PCA or t-SNE (Embedding section).
Use LSTM or GRU rather than plain RNN to mitigate vanishing gradients; GRU is lighter but more prone to overfitting.
Add dropout (0.5) to the GRU sentiment classifier and use stratified train/val/test splits.

terms.definition: decisions and process operations on a corpus (segmentation, lowercasing, lemmatization, stemming) before tokenization
algorithm for extracting features from text that preserves word frequency but ignores position and order
TF multiplied by the logarithm of IDF, where IDF is the ratio of documents in the corpus to documents containing the term
dense, small, real-valued vectors with distributed representation of word meaning, whose size does not grow with vocabulary
self-supervised binary classification (is c in the context of w?) with logistic regression; the classifier weights are the embeddings; introduced by Mikolov 2013
normalized dot product; range -1 to 1, scale-invariant
